text.p: MedPartners Inc, the largest company in the booming U.S. physician practice management market, said it is comfortable with First Call consensus earnings estimates of $0.27 per share for the second quarter and $1.14 per share for 1997.

"We're entirely comfortable with the consensus expectations both for the quarter and for the year," Mark Wagar, president of the Birmingham, Ala.-based firm's western division, said in an interview following remarks at a Piper Jaffray investors conference here.

MedPartners is projected to post revenues this year of $5.75 billion -- a nearly eight-fold increase from just three years ago. Earnings were $0.21 per share in the second quarter of 1996 and $0.86 per share for all of that year.

Explosive growth in revenues and earnings has done little recently to power MedPartners' stock on Wall Street, where analysts said questions linger about the quality and cost of the company's many recent acquisitions.

In addition, the stock is burdened by uncertainty over accounting standards for pooling-of-interests mergers and for the young physician practice management, or PPM, industry as a whole, analysts said.
On the New York Stock Exchange, shares in MedPartners Wednesday closed down 3/8 at 22-3/8, off a 12-month high of 25.

MedPartners emerged in late 1995 as the most aggressive consolidator in the PPM field when it announced its agreement to merge with Mullikin Medical Enterprises in a $360-million pooling-of-interests transaction. Six months later, Pacific Physician Services Inc was acquired in a $332-million pooling.

In May 1996, MedPartners set the industry on its ear by unveiling a $2.5 billion pooling acquisition of the much larger Caremark Inc. Keeping the acquisition machine in high gear, MedPartners in January said it agreed to acquire InPhyNet Medical Management in a $493-million pooling.

Including InPhyNet's business, MedPartners this year will operate in 36 states and be affiliated with 12,000 physicians, whose practices it will in one way of another manage. Despite its size, MedPartners controls less than two percent of the highly fragmented, $200-billion U.S. physician services market.

"MDM has done an outstanding job of assimilating its many acquisitions and has delivered 12 straight quarters of EPS growth at or above expectations," said Piper Jaffray PPM industry analyst Brooks O'Neil.

As managed healthcare sweeps through medicine, physicians are responding by, in many instances, forming large group practices, independent practice associations or other alliances that give them more clout in dealing with powerful HMOs. Often, physicians find that administering large practices is more work than they bargained for, however.

Practice management firms, such as MedPartners, will take over the headaches by buying a practice's assets or reaching a contractual agreement. Such deals give the PPM a piece of the practice's business and give the physician freedom from red tape, as well as still greater clout by being affiliated with a large PPM firm.

"Physicians need to be in organizations with scale and sophistication to meet the challenges of the changing market. PPM companies are well positioned to partner with doctors to help them address these needs," O'Neil said.
Besides MedPartners, other big players in the fast-moving sector include number-two-in-market-capitalization PhyCor Inc, FPA Medical Management Inc and American Oncology Resources Inc.
